objectives: Trace the birth of instrumental seismology from Milne to Lehmann.
Distinguish P, S, and surface waves by their physics and speeds.
Use the S−P travel-time interval to estimate distance to an earthquake source.

slides.title: The birth of instrumental seismology
slides.body:
**Seismology** is the quantitative study of elastic waves that travel through the Earth, almost always generated by **earthquakes** but also by explosions, ocean storms, and human activity. The discipline became a true science only when instruments could record ground motion faithfully.

The central figure is **John Milne (1850–1913)**, a British mining engineer who worked in Meiji-era Japan. Together with colleagues **James Alfred Ewing** and **Thomas Gray**, Milne developed the first practical **horizontal-pendulum seismograph** in the 1880s and founded the **Seismological Society of Japan** in 1880 after a sharp Yokohama earthquake. Milne later built a global network of identical instruments, so for the first time the *same* earthquake could be compared on records from many continents. He is justly called the father of modern seismology.

Analysis of these worldwide records produced a stunning discovery. **Richard Dixon Oldham (1858–1936)**, of the Geological Survey of India, studied the great **1897 Assam earthquake** and then, in a landmark **1906** paper, showed that a seismogram contains three distinct arrivals:

- **Primary (P) waves** — the first, fastest arrival.
- **Secondary (S) waves** — a slower, later arrival.
- **Surface waves** — large, slow, late-arriving waves confined near the surface.

From the way S waves failed to pass through the deep interior, Oldham **inferred the existence of Earth's central core** — a result of breathtaking reach from squiggles on paper.

The story continues with three more giants. **Beno Gutenberg (1889–1960)** precisely located the **core–mantle boundary** at a depth of about $2890$ km (the **Gutenberg discontinuity**, 1913). **Charles Francis Richter (1900–1985)**, working with Gutenberg at **Caltech**, devised the first quantitative earthquake **magnitude scale** in **1935** for Southern California. Finally, the Danish geophysicist **Inge Lehmann (1888–1993)** discovered in **1936** that the core is not uniform: a solid **inner core** sits inside the liquid **outer core**. In barely fifty years, seismologists had mapped the deep Earth without ever touching it — reading its structure from travel times alone.

slides.title: P waves and S waves: two kinds of body wave
slides.body:
Earthquakes radiate two fundamentally different **body waves** that travel through the Earth's volume. The distinction comes from continuum mechanics and was clarified by **Siméon Denis Poisson** in the 1820s.

A **P wave** (primary, or *pressure*) is a **compressional wave**: particles oscillate back and forth *parallel* to the direction of travel, alternately compressing and dilating the rock — exactly like sound in air. Because solids strongly resist compression, P waves are fast and they can travel through **solids and liquids alike**. Their speed depends on the bulk modulus $K$, the shear modulus $\mu$, and density $\rho$:

$$v_P = \sqrt{\frac{K + \tfrac{4}{3}\mu}{\rho}}$$

An **S wave** (secondary, or *shear*) is a **transverse wave**: particles oscillate *perpendicular* to the propagation direction, shearing the rock side to side. Its speed is

$$v_S = \sqrt{\frac{\mu}{\rho}}$$

Because **liquids have no shear strength** ($\mu = 0$), **S waves cannot propagate through a fluid** — the very fact Oldham used to detect the molten outer core. In typical crustal rock $v_P \approx 6$ km/s and $v_S \approx 3.5$ km/s, so P always arrives first; the ratio $v_P/v_S \approx \sqrt{3} \approx 1.73$ for a **Poisson solid** (where $K$ and $\mu$ are comparable). This $\sqrt{3}$ relationship is one of the most useful rules of thumb in seismology.

Key contrasts to remember:

- **P waves**: fastest; compressional; travel through solid *and* liquid; small amplitude on the seismogram.
- **S waves**: slower (roughly $0.6\,v_P$); shear; **blocked by liquids**; larger amplitude than P.
- Both are **body waves**, distinct from the **surface waves** that follow them.

The **interactive visualization** on this slide animates a compressional P wavefront and a transverse S wavefront so you can see the particle motion directly. Watch how the P-wave particles bunch and stretch along the ray, while the S-wave particles whip across it. The growing gap between the two wavefronts, as the faster P pulls ahead, is the physical basis of the distance-finding method we develop next.

slides.title: Surface waves and the S−P distance rule
slides.body:
After the body waves comes the slow, destructive train of **surface waves**, which are guided along the free surface and decay with depth. There are two classic types, named for the British physicists who predicted them:

- **Rayleigh waves** (**Lord Rayleigh**, John William Strutt, **1885**): a retrograde elliptical, rolling motion in the vertical plane — like a swell on the sea — that exists on any free surface.
- **Love waves** (**A. E. H. Love**, **1911**): horizontally polarized shear motion that requires a low-velocity layer over a faster substrate, as the real crust provides.

Surface waves travel slightly slower than S waves but **decay with distance more slowly** (geometric spreading in two dimensions rather than three), so at great range they dominate the record and cause much of the shaking damage in distant cities.

**Locating the source with S−P.** Because $v_P > v_S$, the gap between the P and S arrivals widens steadily with distance from the **hypocenter** (the focus at depth) and its surface projection, the **epicenter**. Let the source be at distance $d$. The travel times are $t_P = d/v_P$ and $t_S = d/v_S$, so the measured **S−P interval** is

$$\Delta t = t_S - t_P = d\left(\frac{1}{v_S} - \frac{1}{v_P}\right).$$

Solving for distance gives the workhorse formula

$$d = \frac{\Delta t}{\dfrac{1}{v_S} - \dfrac{1}{v_P}}.$$

With crustal values $v_P = 6.0$ km/s and $v_S = 3.5$ km/s the bracket is $\tfrac{1}{3.5}-\tfrac{1}{6.0} \approx 0.119$ s/km, so a convenient approximation is $d \approx 8.4\,\Delta t$ km with $\Delta t$ in seconds. The classic rule of thumb — *multiply the S−P time in seconds by about 8* — follows directly.

A single station gives only the **distance** $d$, which defines a circle of possible epicenters. Repeating the measurement at **three or more stations** and intersecting the circles pins down the epicenter — the method of **triangulation** that we will formalize later in the path. This is precisely the data that **John Milne**'s global network first made possible, and that **Beno Gutenberg** and **Inge Lehmann** later exploited to map the deep Earth.

question.question: Why can **S waves** be used to detect that Earth's **outer core** is liquid?
options: S waves travel faster than P waves through liquids, creating a detectable speed-up.
S waves are shear waves, and a liquid has no shear strength ($\mu = 0$), so S waves cannot propagate through the molten outer core and are blocked there.
S waves are compressional and are amplified by the dense liquid core.
S waves carry no energy and therefore reflect off any boundary.
question.explanation: S waves are transverse shear waves with speed $v_S = \sqrt{\mu/\rho}$. A liquid cannot sustain shear stress, so $\mu = 0$ and $v_S = 0$: S waves simply cannot pass through the liquid outer core. Richard Dixon Oldham (1906) used exactly this blockage to infer the core's existence.

hints: Recall $v_S = \sqrt{\mu/\rho}$ and ask what $\mu$ equals in a fluid.
Which wave type is compressional and which is shear?
slides.workedSolution: An S wave is a shear (transverse) wave whose speed is $v_S = \sqrt{\mu/\rho}$, where $\mu$ is the shear modulus. Liquids cannot support a static shear stress, so for a liquid $\mu = 0$ and hence $v_S = 0$ — no S wave can travel through it. The molten outer core therefore blocks direct S waves, which is how Oldham in 1906 inferred a fluid core. P waves, being compressional ($v_P = \sqrt{(K+\tfrac{4}{3}\mu)/\rho}$), still pass because liquids resist compression.

question.question: A station measures an **S−P interval** of $\Delta t = 12$ s. Using the approximation $d \approx 8.4\,\Delta t$ km (with $v_P = 6.0$, $v_S = 3.5$ km/s), what is the approximate distance $d$ to the epicenter, in kilometers?
question.hint: Multiply the S−P time in seconds by about 8.4 km/s.

question.question: For a **Poisson solid**, the ratio $v_P/v_S = \sqrt{3}$. Evaluate $\sqrt{3}$ to two decimal places.
A single station cannot locate an earthquake by itself.
question.prompt: You are on duty at one seismic station and read a clean S−P interval of 9 seconds, giving a source distance of about 75 km. Your supervisor asks you to mark the epicenter on the map, but you can only draw a circle. Explain why one station yields a distance but not a unique location, and describe exactly what additional measurements from neighboring stations would let you pin down the epicenter by triangulation. Mention how Milne's global network of identical instruments made this kind of multi-station comparison possible.

question.question: Match each historical contribution to the correct scientist.
options: Inge Lehmann built the first horizontal-pendulum seismograph in the 1880s.
Charles Richter discovered the solid inner core in 1936.
Richard Dixon Oldham distinguished P, S, and surface waves and inferred Earth's core (1906); Inge Lehmann discovered the solid inner core (1936); Charles Richter devised the magnitude scale (1935).
Beno Gutenberg invented the magnitude scale in 1935 and Richter located the core–mantle boundary.
question.explanation: Oldham (1906) separated the three wave arrivals and inferred the core; Gutenberg (1913) fixed the core–mantle boundary near 2890 km; Richter (1935) created the magnitude scale at Caltech with Gutenberg; Lehmann (1936) found the solid inner core; Milne (1880s) built the early seismographs. Only option C assigns every credit correctly.

hints: Who worked on magnitude, and in what year?
Lehmann is associated with the innermost layer of the Earth.
slides.workedSolution: John Milne built the early horizontal-pendulum seismograph (1880s) and the first global network. Richard Dixon Oldham (1906) distinguished P, S, and surface waves and inferred the core. Beno Gutenberg (1913) located the core–mantle boundary at about 2890 km. Charles Richter (1935) created the magnitude scale with Gutenberg at Caltech. Inge Lehmann (1936) discovered the solid inner core. Option C is the only fully correct mapping.
